transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-11-04 16:00 UTC | Duration: 48m | Attendees: Maya Chen, Ethan Park, Rita Gomez (Redwood) — Anya Patel, Marcus Lee, Sofia Rivera, Julian Ko (Copperhead)

Summary: Quick demo of Redwood Optimize console and cost workbook. Walked through a prefetched lookahead strategy for Copperhead's short-chat use case, explored batch/concurrency scenarios and KV TTL tradeoffs. Agreed next steps to run sandbox with real traces.

00:00 Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro — I'm Maya on the AE side, with Ethan and Rita from Solutions. we have, um, about 45 minutes. Is that still good?
00:07 Anya Patel: Yep, that's perfect. We wanted to focus on caching/prefetch because tokens are our largest cost line right now.
00:14 Maya Chen: Great, we'll go through the Optimize console, show the cost workbook, and then a couple of sandbox scenarios — low concurrency and high concurrency. If we have time, we'll touch on security and deployment questions.
00:24 Ethan Park: Real quick — Marcus, Sofia, can you confirm your latency SLOs and throughput so I can tailor the batching examples?
00:31 Marcus Lee: We're targeting p50 under 60 ms and p99 under 200 ms for the inference leg. Peak RPS is around 1,200 but realistically average is 240 with spikes.
00:40 Ethan Park: Awesome, that helps. So given that distribution, prefetch & prefix cache can save a lot if you have repeated session prompts.
00:48 Rita Gomez: I'll share my screen — showing the Optimize console. Top left is the model profile, token cost assumptions, and the savings simulator.
00:56 [screen share noise]
01:05 Rita Gomez: Alright, first slide: baseline without caching. We use Copperhead sample — single-turn average prompt size ~120 tokens, responses ~220 tokens. At current throughput that maps to roughly X tokens / minute and projected monthly spend on hosted is about — the workbook shows line items — sorry, the transcription sometimes truncates numbers — but you can see the per-token unit cost assumptions.
01:30 Julian Ko: Quick Q — when you say 'prefetch' are you doing full response generation ahead of time or just prefix KV priming? How destructive is it to latency?
01:38 Ethan Park: Good question. We're talking about lookahead prefetch which primes the KV cache with likely next-token contexts. It's not full generation in most cases, it's more like issuing a lightweight prefix step so the heavier attention compute on subsequent tokens hits cache and can be batched. That reduces per-token runtime and enables bigger batches without pushing p99 over budget.
01:55 Anya Patel: So it's like speculative warmup? what if predictions are wrong — do we waste tokens and pay for them?
02:02 Ethan Park: Yes, there's a cost tradeoff. Our workbook models hit-rate vs speculative cost. If your hit-rate is high (like >45% on multi-turn flows) you get net savings. if not, you can lower the lookahead depth or apply it only for specific UX flows.
02:14 Marcus Lee: For our chat assistant the flows are pretty templated — about 60% repeatable. we also have sessionization by user id for short windows.
02:23 Maya Chen: That aligns well. Let's demo a fast scenario: Scenario A — high-prefetch depth (2 tokens lookahead), TTL of KV entries = 120s, batch window 25 ms, concurrency cap 12. Scenario B — conservative prefetch: depth 1, TTL 30s, batch window 10 ms.
02:41 [keyboard clacks]
02:46 Rita Gomez: Pulling up the console simulation. Here's the baseline cost line. flipping to Scenario A — you can see token units used drop about 28% in the sim, but tail latency creeping up at peak if concurrency spikes.
03:02 Anya Patel: Can you show the sim numbers? like cost per 1M tokens?
03:06 Rita Gomez: Sure — workbook cell: baseline hosted ~ $4.2k per 1M tokens (example unit), Scenario A effective net ~ $3.05k per 1M tokens after prefetch savings and batching uplift. Scenario B nets about $3.7k per 1M. Those are illustrative — we should re-run with Copperhead's exact unit prices.
03:25 Sofia Rivera: Wait, you mentioned batching uplift — how does that interact with streaming and early token emission? We stream tokens in product.
03:33 Ethan Park: Right — streaming complicates large batch windows since we want early partial responses. Redwood's runtime supports hybrid: small batch window for first tokens (to keep start latency low) and adaptive batching for mid/late tokens. Prefetch mainly helps the KV heavy part so you can maintain streaming while still batching the heavy compute. It's an engineering knob in the console.
03:53 Anya Patel: Are there any quantized model variants we should consider? We do have some tolerance for small quality regressions.
03:59 Rita Gomez: Yes — Optimize will suggest lower precision variants and show quality regression risk. For chat with your templated prompts, 4-bit quantization with certain kernels is often viable; the workbook models quality penalty as a toggle.
04:11 Marcus Lee: Security: we are SOC2 compliant and need any cloud vendor to allow us to bring our own KMS for keys. That matters for Private/Dedicated.
04:19 Maya Chen: Totally — Copperhead's private deploy roadmap is covered. For Hosted we have managed key options, but for Private/Dedicated we can integrate with KMS/HSM and preserve audit logs. We'll attach the security deck after.
04:29 Sofia Rivera: Also need data residency — EU region only for some customers.
04:33 Maya Chen: Noted — routing policies can pin requests to region and Dedicated pools.
04:38 [brief pause]
04:42 Ethan Park: Back to cost math — lookahead hit-rate is the variable with biggest leverage. If you can annotate sessions that are 'repeatable' we can auto-enable prefetch only for those. The console supports tag-based routing.
04:56 Anya Patel: For copperhead, we have three flow types: templated chatbot (60% repeatable), search-based retrieval assistant (low repeat), and code-assist (high variability). We'll likely enable prefetch only for templated chat first.
05:09 Rita Gomez: Good plan. I'll toggle the simulator to only apply prefetch to 55% of traffic and show blended savings. [sim flicker] That yields about 18% net token reduction and keeps p99 safely under 200ms in the sim when TTLs are tuned to 45s.
05:30 Marcus Lee: TTLs — what's the operational cost if TTLs are long? do we risk stale session context?
05:36 Ethan Park: TTLs only control KV cache lifetime, not user-visible state. If your app requires strict freshness, you should choose shorter TTLs or clear session keys on certain events. Longer TTLs give more cache hits but also more memory footprint; Dedicated pools can be sized accordingly.
05:49 Anya Patel: Can Redwood autoscale cache nodes independent of model workers?
05:52 Rita Gomez: Yes. Cache layer can scale separately; we expose metrics in Console for cache hit-rate, mem usage, evictions. The Optimize suggestions include a cache sizing recommendation based on observed cardinality in your traces.
06:04 [15s pause]
06:20 Ethan Park: Let's walk through a small concrete worked example — we pulled a sample trace from Copperhead (sanitized) — replaying a subset in sandbox: 1M requests, baseline tokens ~340M, average latency baseline 95 ms, p99 180 ms. With lookahead depth 1 and TTL 45s, tokens dropped by ~21% and p99 moved to 170 ms; batch window tuned to 15 ms.
06:44 Anya Patel: nice. How confident are you in these numbers given different concurrency distributions?
06:48 Ethan Park: We run sensitivity analysis — the workbook includes low/medium/high concurrency curves. At higher spikes (2x peak) the savings remain but p99 can degrade unless we route overflow to Dedicated or fallback model. Redwood supports automatic fallback to a cheaper lower-SLO variant.
07:05 Julian Ko: On fallbacks — is that per-request policy? We need deterministic guarantees for some customers.
07:10 Maya Chen: Yes, per-route policies. You can set hard SLOs and have canary/routing policies: e.g., if model latency > 220ms or queue length > 50, route to fallback model or another region. All configured in Console.
07:21 Marcus Lee: For the pilot, we want benchmarks on our real traffic. What's the minimum data you need?
07:26 Ethan Park: Ideally 7 days of logs, with anonymized user identifiers and timestamps, plus 50 representative prompt examples. With that we can run sims and a small sandbox replay.
07:35 Anya Patel: We can do that. we'll scrub PII first.
07:38 Maya Chen: Great. Rita, can you also show the Cost Workbook export and the token line-item breakdown?
07:44 Rita Gomez: Exporting now — you get per-route token counts, batching effect, prefetch speculative spend, and net savings. There's also a sensitivity tab where we vary hit-rate and TTL and show break-even points.
07:56 Anya Patel: In the sensitivity tab, what's the break-even hit-rate for lookahead depth 2?
07:59 Rita Gomez: For your prompt sizes it's about 42–46%. Below that, the speculative token cost outweighs savings from batching. Depth 1 is cheaper to experiment with.
08:10 Sofia Rivera: A couple infra questions — does Redwood's runtime require us to open direct inbound connections? we run in VPC.
08:16 Maya Chen: For Private you'll run the runtime in your VPC; control plane calls are outbound. For Dedicated we offer VPC peering and private networking. We can work with your security team on the exact network topology.
08:29 Marcus Lee: Also curious on observability — can we tag tokens to customer_id for cost attribution?
08:34 Rita Gomez: Yep — token-level attribution and per-route dashboards are standard. We can also export a CSV or push into your metrics stack.
08:41 [background cough]
08:47 Ethan Park: Quick demo of the policy engine — setting TTL to 45s for session-prefetch route, enabling prefetch only for 'templated' tag, batch window at 15 ms, concurrency cap 12, fallback to smaller variant when queue > 40. Save policy.
09:05 Anya Patel: Can you show how we schedule gradual rollout? We want canary 5% -> 25% -> 100%.
09:10 Rita Gomez: Console supports rollout steps with automatic metric gates; we'll define p99 and error-rate gates. If a gate fails, rollout pauses and we can notify slack via webhook.
09:23 Julian Ko: On pricing, can you ballpark Dedicated commit levels for our scale?
09:28 Maya Chen: Ballpark only: given your average concurrency and token usage, we'd estimate a mid-tier Dedicated pool with 8 GPUs. That'd be a monthly commit — we'll put exact numbers in the workbook once we have your traffic. Hosted per-token still possible for initial pilot.
09:42 Anya Patel: For the pilot timeline — we'd like a quick win in 2 weeks if possible.
09:46 Maya Chen: Sounds doable. We'll run the sandbox sim within next 5 business days and deliver a cost-savings workbook.
09:52 Marcus Lee: Anything about compliance we should read now?
09:55 Maya Chen: I'll send the security pack after the call — SOC2, encryption, KMS integration notes, and a private deployment checklist.
10:03 [brief cross talk]
10:10 Rita Gomez: I'm toggling advanced knobs — lookahead sampling mode, warm-up thresholds, and prefetch gating by user segment. All of these reduce speculative spend if you only apply prefetch to high-confidence segments.
10:24 Anya Patel: Could Redwood run the warm-up for only authenticated sessions? we have lots of anon traffic.
10:29 Ethan Park: Yes — apply tag-based filters; prefetched requests require a session id. For anonymous flows we recommend shorter TTLs or no prefetch.
10:38 Sofia Rivera: Anything we should watch for operationally — evictions, memory pressure?
10:42 Rita Gomez: Monitor cache hit-rate, evictions per minute, and median item size. We'll recommend cache capacity with some headroom. Evictions are expected and fine; it's just a throughput/latency tradeoff.
10:52 Anya Patel: Good. I'm comfortable moving forward with a pilot for templated chat only.
10:56 Maya Chen: Great — recap of next steps: Maya to send workbook, Ethan to run sandbox, Copperhead to send traces — timelines in the action items. We'll do a technical deep-dive after the sandbox.
11:08 Marcus Lee: Sounds good. thank you all.
11:11 Maya Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with calendar invites and links.

Action items (recap):
- Maya Chen: cost workbook + security pack (by 2026-11-06)
- Ethan Park: sandbox simulations using Copperhead traces (by 2026-11-09)
- Anya / Copperhead: provide 7 days of anonymized logs + 3 canonical prompts (by 2026-11-08)
- Sofia: confirm KMS/HSM constraints in writing (by 2026-11-10)

End of transcript.
